audience: undergraduate computer science; spoken explanation of 1-3 minutes

key_points.text: Both are transport-layer protocols that run over IP and use port numbers to reach applications.
key_points.partial_if: says they are 'network protocols' without the transport layer or ports

key_points.text: TCP is connection-oriented (a three-way handshake sets up a connection); UDP is connectionless and just sends datagrams.
key_points.partial_if: says TCP 'connects' and UDP does not, with no detail

key_points.text: TCP gives reliable, ordered delivery using sequence numbers, acknowledgements and retransmission; UDP is best effort, with no guarantee of delivery, order or duplicate removal.
key_points.partial_if: says TCP is 'reliable' and UDP is 'unreliable' without saying how or what is guaranteed

key_points.text: TCP has flow control and congestion control; UDP has neither.
key_points.partial_if: mentions one of the two, or 'TCP controls the speed' vaguely

key_points.text: UDP has lower overhead (8-byte header vs at least 20 bytes, no handshake, no waiting for retransmissions), so lower latency; TCP is a byte stream, UDP keeps message boundaries.
key_points.partial_if: says UDP is 'faster' or 'lighter' without the reason

key_points.text: Typical uses: TCP for the web, email and file transfer; UDP for DNS, live audio/video, VoIP and online games, where timeliness matters more than perfect delivery.
key_points.partial_if: gives uses for only one protocol, or examples without the reason

misconceptions.text: UDP is less secure than TCP (neither protocol encrypts data; security comes from TLS, DTLS and similar).
UDP packets travel through the network faster than TCP packets.
TCP guarantees that data always arrives, even if the connection breaks.
